flagged.location: Remarks, “The condition is symmetric in H and its conjugates”
flagged.evidence: It says the condition is equivalent to requiring H∩gHg⁻¹={1} only when gHg⁻¹≠H. In G=C4 with H=<a²>, every conjugate equals H, so that condition is vacuous; the original condition fails for g=a∉H because H∩gHg⁻¹=H≠{1}.

flagged.location: Definition, “What is and is not claimed”
flagged.evidence: The text says y^g=x^(gu) and “gu∈P^g whenever u∈P.” The latter is false: in S3 take P=< (12) >, g=(123), and u=e; then gu=g has order 3 while P^g has order 2. The conjugating element in P^g is gug⁻¹.

The piecewise formula gives a value when π is not isomorphic to σ or when σ=π, and clarifies that σ=π means the very same representation. It leaves equivalent but distinct representations uncovered. For the trivial compact group, take equivalent trivial irreducible representations on distinct one-dimensional spaces and unit vectors; both coefficients are 1 and their convolution is 1, but neither branch applies.
The note says counting measure is “still σ-finite.” For an uncountable discrete group, every finite-measure set is finite, and a countable union of finite sets cannot cover the group.

The summary says the induced class function θ^G “has norm one.” In lem-frobenius-character-extension-is-irreducible, proof steps 2.2–3.1 give ||Ind θ||²=1+φ(1)², while it is the adjusted function ~φ=Ind θ+φ(1)1_G that has norm one.

It claims ||R_g f||₁=Δ_G(g)^{1/2}||f||₁. But R_g f(x)=Δ_G(g)^{1/2}f(xg), and the cited scaling is ∫|f(xg)|dμ=Δ_G(g⁻¹)||f||₁, so the factor is Δ_G(g)^{-1/2}. For the affine group with g=(2,0), the claimed factor is 1/√2 and the actual factor is √2.

From “t^n∈Δ_G(G) for every n∈N” and boundedness, it concludes t=1. This does not exclude 0<t<1, whose positive powers are bounded; the argument needs also to apply boundedness to t⁻¹, which is in the subgroup image.

It says the uniformly Cauchy sequence u_n*f “converges uniformly to its L1-limit u*f.” Uniform Cauchy convergence gives a uniform limit, but the proof does not identify that limit with the L1 class limit; a short subsequence argument gives equality almost everywhere.
It says of the two nonidentity elements of A3 that “their product is the other one.” They are a=(012) and a⁻¹=(021), and their product is the identity, not the other nonidentity element.
It states (z^u)^v=z^{uv} for z^u=uzu⁻¹. Direct multiplication gives (z^u)^v=vuz u⁻¹v⁻¹=z^{vu}; these differ in general when u and v do not commute.

The proof fixes a Borel E with μ(E)>0 and infers c(gh)=c(g)c(h) from comparing scalar multiples of μ(E). Such E could have infinite measure, in which case the equality does not determine the scalars; choose E with 0<μ(E)<∞, available from a positive-measure compact set.
